strengths: The paper identifies a clear and realistic problem: pre-trained text-to-image diffusion models struggle with standard textual conditions in robotic control tasks due to the domain gap between web images and simulated environments, and the need for frame-by-frame dynamic guidance.

The proposed ORCA framework presents a simple yet effective way to inject task-level information (learnable task prompts) and frame-level fine-grained visual details (visual prompts) into the diffusion model's cross-attention layers.

Strong quantitative results across three major simulated robotic suites (DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit) show that ORCA consistently outperforms both task-agnostic baselines (CLIP, VC-1, SCR) and task-adaptive prompt tuning baselines (CoOp, TADP).

Extensive analyses are provided, including insightful cross-attention visualizations that justify why text conditions fail and how task/visual prompts succeed, alongside layer selection and timestep ablations.
weaknesses: As shown in Table 7, ORCA incurs a significant latency increase (48ms compared to 11ms for VC-1 and 26ms for SCR). In real-world robotic control, a 48ms feature extraction latency could heavily constrain real-time policy execution (which typically runs at 20-50Hz). This computational bottleneck and its implications on deployment should be more thoroughly discussed.

The visual prompts in ORCA are generated by passing observations through a pre-trained DINOv2 encoder. Since DINOv2 is already an exceptionally strong visual representation, it is not entirely clear how much of the performance gain is due to the diffusion model's representation versus DINOv2's strong localized features. An ablation or baseline that directly utilizes DINOv2 features for policy learning (without the Stable Diffusion backbone) would clarify the exact value added by the diffusion model.

The evaluation is performed solely in simulated environments (MetaWorld, DMC, Adroit). Given that the paper emphasizes the 'domain gap' between real-world training data and control environments, validating the method on a physical robot platform would significantly strengthen the claims of robustness and real-world applicability.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and critical failure mode of pre-trained text-to-image diffusion models in robotic control: standard textual prompts suffer from grounding issues and domain gaps in simulation environments, which can even degrade policy learning compared to the null condition.

The proposed ORCA framework successfully addresses this issue by introducing a hybrid prompting scheme combining learnable task-specific tokens (optimized end-to-end via behavior cloning) and frame-specific visual tokens extracted from a pre-trained vision encoder.

Experiments are thorough, spanning 12 tasks across three major benchmarks (DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit), showing consistent and substantial improvements over task-agnostic baselines (CLIP, VC-1, SCR) and prompting baselines (CoOp, TADP).

Excellent qualitative analysis and cross-attention map visualizations clarify how the task prompts focus on global targets and visual prompts capture frame-specific movements and fine-grained structures.
Honest and clear ablation studies in the appendix, including the effect of timesteps, individual prompting components, and layer selection.
weaknesses: High computational complexity and inference latency: As shown in Table 7, ORCA has a latency of 48ms per step, which is more than 4x slower than VC-1 (11ms) and nearly 2x slower than SCR (26ms). This high latency limits the applicability of the method in real-world, high-frequency robotic control (e.g., >= 50Hz).

Decoupling the role of DINOv2: Since DINOv2 is used as the visual prompt encoder, and DINOv2 itself is already a highly capable pre-trained visual representation model, it is crucial to verify how much of the performance gain is due to the conditioned Stable Diffusion representations versus simply utilizing DINOv2 features. A baseline directly using DINOv2 features for the control policy is missing.
Evaluation is restricted to low-data imitation learning (2-5 demonstrations). It remains unclear how these representations behave under larger datasets or online reinforcement learning setups.

strengths: Insightful Analysis of Text Conditions: The paper provides an interesting case study (Section 4.1, Figure 3) analyzing why naive text conditions (even from state-of-the-art VLMs like Gemini 2.5) can degrade performance in simulated robotic control due to poor text-to-image grounding and domain gaps.
Effective Prompting Strategy: Proposing a hybrid of learnable task prompts and dense visual prompts successfully addresses the spatial and temporal grounding limitations of frozen representations.

Comprehensive Evaluation: The method is validated on three standard robotic control suites (DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit) across 12 diverse tasks, showing consistent improvements over several visual representation baselines.
Detailed Ablation Studies: The authors provide thorough ablations on layer selection, timestep selection, and prompt components, which helps understand the design choices of the proposed framework.
weaknesses: Missing DINOv2 Baseline: DINOv2 is used as the external vision encoder to extract features for the visual prompts. Since DINOv2 is known to be an extremely strong visual representation for robotic control on its own, it is crucial to include a baseline that uses DINOv2 features directly for policy learning. Without this baseline, it is difficult to determine how much of the performance improvement is due to the interaction with the Stable Diffusion model versus simply leveraging the powerful representations of DINOv2.

High Latency and Computational Overhead: Table 7 shows that ORCA has a latency of 48ms, which is significantly slower than VC-1 (11ms) and SCR (26ms). For real-world robotic control, a 48ms perception latency is a significant bottleneck (limiting the system to <20Hz even before accounting for policy inference and controller delays).

The Role of the Diffusion Model at t=0: Table 6 shows that setting the diffusion timestep t=0 yields the best performance. Since no noise is added at t=0, the Stable Diffusion U-Net is essentially treated as a standard, deterministic image encoder rather than leveraging its generative denoising properties. This further raises the question of whether a standard large vision model of similar size would be more effective and computationally efficient.

Clarification on Training Details: While Section 6.2 mentions that most of the parameters added are the frozen parameters from DINOv2, the manuscript would benefit from a clearer, explicit list or diagram of which components are frozen and which are trainable (e.g., projection layers, task prompts, policy head) during the behavior cloning phase.

strengths: Insightful motivation and analysis: The paper systematically investigates why conventional textual conditioning of pre-trained diffusion models fails in robotic control, using cross-attention visualizations to clearly illustrate the domain/grounding gap.

Elegant and parameter-efficient design: ORCA leverages learnable task prompts and frame-level visual prompts to adapt frozen diffusion models dynamically, avoiding the catastrophic overfitting typical of full fine-tuning on limited robotic demonstration data.

Strong empirical performance: ORCA establishes a new state-of-the-art across multiple widely-used benchmarks (DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit, and LIBERO-Long), consistently outperforming both task-agnostic visual representations (CLIP, VC-1, SCR) and existing prompting baselines.

Rigorous ablation and qualitative validation: The manuscript provides thorough analyses of layer selection, diffusion timesteps, visual encoders, and includes high-quality cross-attention visualizations showing that the learned prompts successfully attend to task-relevant areas.
weaknesses: Inference latency and computational overhead: As shown in Table F, the inference latency of ORCA is 48ms, which is significantly slower than VC-1 (11ms) and SCR (26ms). For high-frequency, real-world robotic control loops (e.g., 50-100Hz), this latency could pose a practical bottleneck, and the paper would benefit from discussing this limitation or potential acceleration strategies.

Pipeline complexity: The visual prompt mechanism relies on an external visual encoder (DINOv2). While Table C shows that using internal SD-VAE latents is still viable, the optimal performance heavily depends on utilizing another large frozen foundation model, which increases the overall model footprint.

Lack of real-world physical robot evaluation: All experiments are conducted entirely within simulated environments. Evaluating on a real robot would strengthen the paper by demonstrating how the prompt-conditioned representation handles physical camera noise, lighting variations, and real-time controller limits.

strengths: The paper presents a thorough and systematic exploration of different conditioning methods (text prompts, learnable task prompts, and frame-specific visual prompts) for diffusion-based representations in robotic control, identifying the limitations of naive text conditioning with clear visual evidence (cross-attention maps).

The proposed method, ORCA, consistently and significantly outperforms strong task-agnostic (CLIP, VC-1) and task-specific (SCR, CoOp, TADP) baselines across multiple benchmarks (DeepMind Control, MetaWorld, Adroit, and LIBERO-Long).

The paper includes comprehensive and rigorous ablation studies, including layer-wise U-Net selection, diffusion backbones (SD 1.5, SVD, SD 3.0), different visual encoders for visual prompts (DINOv2, SigLIP, CLIP, SD-VAE), and timestep choices.
The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, with highly illustrative figures (especially Figures 3 and 4) and an intuitive progression from motivation to methodology.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty of the proposed components is somewhat incremental, as soft/learnable prompt tuning (e.g., CoOp) and visual conditioning from external encoders (e.g., TADP) are already widely explored in general vision tasks.

High computational complexity and inference latency: As shown in Table F, ORCA has a latency of 48ms and contains 480.1M parameters, which is significantly slower than standard visual encoders (e.g., VC-1 at 11ms). This latency limit (~20 Hz) could be a major bottleneck for high-frequency, real-world robotic control loops.

The evaluation is restricted entirely to simulated environments. Lacking real-world robot experiments makes it difficult to assess how the proposed conditioning handles physical dynamics, real-world visual domain gaps, and actual deployment constraints.

The framework relies heavily on two massive frozen foundation models simultaneously (Stable Diffusion and DINOv2), greatly increasing the memory footprint and implementation overhead compared to standard single-encoder paradigms.

strengths: Well-motivated exploration: The paper provides a clear analysis of why standard textual conditioning fails in text-to-image diffusion models when applied to simulated robotic control tasks, highlighting the domain gap and noisy cross-attention.

Comprehensive evaluation: The method is tested across multiple standard robotic benchmarks (DeepMind Control, MetaWorld, Adroit, and LIBERO-Long) and demonstrates consistent, significant improvements over previous task-agnostic and task-adaptive baselines.

Excellent qualitative and quantitative analysis: The paper features detailed ablation studies on individual components, layer selection, choice of external visual encoders, diffusion timesteps, and provides insightful cross-attention visualizations.
weaknesses: Computational and Latency Overhead: Using Stable Diffusion v1.5 along with an external visual encoder (DINOv2) introduces a significant computational burden. As shown in Table F, the inference latency increases to 48ms, which could limit its real-time deployment on physical robots requiring high-frequency control loops.

Underutilization of the 'Diffusion' Process: The optimal timestep is found to be $t=0$. This essentially uses the Stable Diffusion U-Net as a standard, deterministic deep visual feature extractor rather than leveraging any generative or multi-step denoising properties inherent to diffusion processes.

Incremental Technical Novelty: The approach of using learnable soft prompts (similar to CoOp) and integrating dense features from an external encoder is a well-established pattern in the broader vision-language literature, making the technical novelty somewhat incremental.
